articles.summary: Employee Management Pension Contributions in Nigeria: A Practical Guide for Employers and HR Teams Oluwakemi Adesina September 24, 2026 Most Nigerian employers can state the pension figures: 10 percent from the company and 8 percent from the employee. But pension contributions in Nigeria involve more than getting those two percentages right. The real work is in knowing what counts as monthly emolument, calculating the correct amounts, remitting them on time, and keeping records that can support the numbers later. This guide explains how the Contributory Pension Scheme works, what employers and employees are responsible for, how to calculate contributions, and what businesses should keep in place for pension compliance. What Is the Contributory Pension Scheme in Nigeria? The Contributory Pension Scheme Nigeria operates through each employee’s Retirement Savings Account (RSA), which belongs to the employee and remains with them when they change jobs. The National Pension Commission (PenCom) regulates the pension industry and supervises the organisations responsible for managing and holding pension assets. Two organisations are particularly important: A Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) manages and invests the funds in an employee’s RSA. A Pension Fund Custodian (PFC) holds the pension assets and receives contributions remitted by employers. The Retirement Savings Account is therefore central to the system. It gives each employee an individual record of their accumulated pension contributions. Who Is Responsible for Pension Contributions? Both the employer and employee have responsibilities under the CPS. For most employees covered by the scheme, the minimum contribution is 18 percent of monthly emoluments: 10 percent from the employer 8 percent from the employee The employer deducts the employee’s portion from salary and remits it together with the employer’s contribution. Employees are responsible for providing accurate pension information, including their existing RSA details where applicable. Employers, meanwhile, need to maintain accurate employee records, make the required deductions, add the employer contribution, and ensure that the combined amount is remitted within the prescribed period. How Pension Contributions Nigeria Employers Make Are Calculated The minimum contribution rates apply to monthly emoluments, rather than automatically applying to every component of gross salary. Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, monthly emoluments comprise the employee’s basic salary, housing allowance and transport allowance. For example, a manager whose qualifying monthly emoluments total ₦450,000. The calculation would be: Employee contribution: 8% × ₦450,000 = ₦36,000 Employer contribution: 10% × ₦450,000 = ₦45,000 Total monthly contribution: ₦81,000 An employer may also elect to bear the full contribution rather than deducting the employee’s portion. PenCom’s guidance provides for an employer that takes on the full contribution responsibility, subject to the applicable minimum contribution requirement. How Employers Remit Pension Contributions in Nigeria Once payroll is processed, the employer should: Calculate the employee and employer contributions. Deduct the employee’s contribution from salary. Prepare the pension schedule. Remit the combined contribution through the applicable PFC process. Keep evidence of the remittance. Reconcile the amount remitted against the payroll records. Under the CPS, pension contributions must be remitted within 7 working days of paying the employee’s salary. Pension Records Every Employer Should Maintain Good pension compliance for employers depends partly on being able to show how each contribution was calculated and where it went. Employers should maintain records such as: Employee RSA and pension identification details Monthly contribution schedules Salary and monthly-emolument records Employee pension deductions Evidence of pension remittances PFA-related documentation Group Life Insurance documentation Reconciliation between payroll records and pension remittances That becomes particularly useful when an employer needs to respond to a compliance request or apply for a Pension Clearance Certificate. Common Pension Contribution Mistakes Businesses Make Mistake What happens Why it matters Wrong calculation base The contribution rate is applied to the wrong salary figure. Contributions may be understated. Outdated rates Payroll continues using an old contribution structure. The business may under-remit. Delayed remittance Contributions are held after salary has been paid. The employer may become liable for the outstanding contribution and applicable penalty. Poor records Schedules or remittance evidence are incomplete. Reconciliation becomes difficult. Payroll mismatch The amount calculated differs from the amount remitted. Errors can remain unresolved until a compliance review. Pension Compliance and Employer Responsibilities Making the monthly payment is only one part of pension compliance. A Pension Clearance Certificate (PCC) provides evidence of an organisation’s pension compliance and may be required in certain contracting and procurement situations. PenCom’s current process uses its Employer Hub for new PCC applications. Employers should therefore keep their contribution schedules, employee information, remittance evidence and other required compliance documents organised before a certificate is needed. Pension compliance for employers also extends beyond the monthly calculation. HR and finance teams need a process for reviewing employee records, checking deductions, reconciling remittances and responding to requests from the relevant authorities. Pension is also one part of a wider statutory compliance picture. Depending on the business and its workforce, employers may have other obligations relating to payroll taxes, employee insurance and statutory employment contributions. How Payroll Technology Can Support Pension Management Many pension errors begin when payroll calculation, deductions, remittance and record-keeping Payroll technology can reduce that fragmentation by keeping employee information, payroll calculations and payment records within a more structured workflow. For HR and finance teams, when employee salary records, deductions and payroll reports are organised consistently, it becomes easier to reconcile payroll with pension records and investigate discrepancies. articles.summary: Por Ana M. Cintrón, fundadora y directora ejecutiva de Causa Local Hablar de é xito empresarial es inspirador, pero hablar de los errores que hicieron posible ese é xito puede ser aún má s valioso. Detr ás de cada negocio que hoy admiramos hay decisiones que no salieron como se esperaba, oportunidades perdidas, tropiezos y momentos de incertidumbre. Sin embargo, son precisamente esas experiencias las que fortalecen el liderazgo y preparan a los empresarios para crecer. En Causa Local, a trav é s de iniciativas como el evento Fuckup Nights San Juan, junto a Piloto 151, hemos comprobado que compartir historias de fracaso no significa celebrar los errores, sino cambiar la conversación sobre estos. Cuando un empresario habla con honestidad sobre un reto que logró superar, otros pueden aprender sin tener que recorrer el mismo camino. Las siguientes experiencias, compartidas por empresarios puertorriqueños, reflejan una realidad que muchas veces pasa desapercibida: el fracaso no es el final del camino, sino una oportunidad para construir empresas má s preparadas . El valor de construir relaciones, no solo contratos Para Isamar Acevedo, fundadora de la agencia de mercadeo y comunicaciones iA Comm Studio , uno de los aprendizajes más importantes llegó despu é s de perder una cuenta importante para su negocio. El problema no fue la calidad del trabajo; el servicio había sido excelente. El verdadero error fue depender de una sola persona dentro de la organización. Cuando ese contacto dejó de influir en las decisiones, tambi é n desapareció la posibilidad de renovar el contrato. Esa experiencia transformó su estrategia comercial. Hoy procura construir relaciones con diferentes personas dentro de cada empresa y asegurarse de que el valor de su trabajo sea conocido por quienes participan en la toma de decisiones. Su historia nos recuerda que los resultados abren puertas, pero las relaciones sólidas son las que ayudan a mantenerlas abiertas. No toda oportunidad representa una buena inversión Cuando PRuK Bakehouse apenas comenzaba, recibió una invitación para participar en un mercado artesanal. Con entusiasmo aceptaron, pero, al llegar, descubrieron que el evento tenía poca promoción y escasa asistencia. Despu é s de horas de trabajo, vendieron ú nicamente tres panes. Aunque la experiencia resultó frustrante, les permiti ó redefinir la manera en que seleccionan los eventos en los que participan. Hoy evalúan cuidadosamente la trayectoria de cada mercado, su presencia en redes sociales, el perfil de los asistentes y si realmente representa una oportunidad para conectar con su cliente ideal. El aprendizaje fue claro: crecer tambi é n implica aprender a elegir dónde invertir el tiempo y los recursos. No todas las oportunidades generan resultados. Cuando el é xito llega má s r ápido de lo esperado Muchas empresas sueñan con vender más. Sin embargo, crecer aceleradamente tambi é n puede convertirse en un reto operativo. Eso fue lo que vivió Yayi P é rez durante la residencia de Bad Bunny en Puerto Rico. La demanda por sus productos aumentó tanto que el taller no podía producir al ritmo que los clientes esperaban. Aunque perdió algunas ventas, decidió no comprometer la calidad de su trabajo y enfocó sus esfuerzos en ofrecer una experiencia de servicio excepcional. Poco despu é s enfrentó otro desafío cuando finalizó el contrato del local donde operaba su tienda física. A pesar de mantener una clientela fiel, la falta de un espacio comercial continúa impactando sus ventas presenciales. Su experiencia demuestra que algunos retos no dependen de malas decisiones. Existen factores externos que todo empresario debe aprender a enfrentar con creatividad, flexibilidad y una comunicación constante con sus clientes. Delegar tambi é n es parte de emprender Christian Rivera, fundador de 183Grados en Bayamón, reconoce que uno de sus mayores errores fue intentar hacerlo todo solo. Durante los primeros años asumió la producción, las ventas, el mercadeo y la administración de su negocio, sin contar con una cuenta comercial ni el apoyo de un profesional en contabilidad. Como resultado, enfrentó multas relacionadas con el manejo del IVU y comprendió que administrar un negocio requiere mucho más que pasión. Con el tiempo contrató un contador, organizó sus finanzas y comenzó a delegar responsabilidades. Su historia demuestra que pedir ayuda no representa una debilidad. Por el contrario, es una decisión estrat é gica para construir una empresa más só lida. Aprender para seguir creciendo Aunque las historias son diferentes, todas comparten un mismo mensaje: los errores no definen el futuro de un negocio. Lo que realmente marca la diferencia es la capacidad de aprender, adaptarse y tomar mejores decisiones a partir de la experiencia. Para quienes están construyendo o haciendo crecer una empresa, estos testimonios dejan varias lecciones prácticas: diversificar las relaciones comerciales, evaluar cuidadosamente las oportunidades, fortalecer la estructura financiera desde el inicio, prepararse para crecer de forma sostenible y rodearse de personas que aporten conocimientos especializados. Emprender implica asumir riesgos, y ningún empresario está exento de equivocarse. Sin embargo, cada desafío superado fortalece la experiencia y permite desarrollar negocios más preparados para el futuro. Quizás por eso el verdadero fracaso no sea cometer un error, sino dejar pasar la oportunidad de aprender de é l. Porque detrás de cada empresa que hoy inspira a otros, existe una historia de resiliencia, perseverancia y crecimiento que comenzó con un tropiezo. En Causa Local creemos que emprender también implica aprender a navegar la incertidumbre, los errores y esos momentos en los que las cosas no salen como esperábamos. articles.summary: Toggle MRAM or STT-MRAM? Start With the Application stephanie.quinn Thu, 24 Sep 2026 - 11:38 Click Here to Read PDF Version Image Toggle MRAM and spin-transfer torque MRAM (STT-MRAM) share the characteristics that draw designers to MRAM in the first place: data retention without power, fast access and the ability to rewrite data without the erase-before-write operations associated with flash memory. They are still different design choices. Everspin's Toggle portfolio serves 3.3V serial and parallel designs across densities from 128Kb to 32Mb. Everspin's xSPI (Expanded Serial Peripheral Interface) STT-MRAM operates at 1.8V and extends the MRAM portfolio into higher densities and faster serial interfaces. Depending on the system, interface, voltage or density may narrow the choices before other specifications even come into play. That is also why STT-MRAM should not be viewed simply as the newer replacement for Toggle. Both remain useful because they solve different memory problems. Where Toggle MRAM fits Toggle MRAM has a long commercial production history and remains widely used in embedded systems that need persistent memory, frequent writes, endurance, long data retention and reliability and long product lifecycles. Everspin's current Toggle portfolio spans 128Kb to 32Mb across serial and asynchronous parallel products. Interfaces include SPI, Quad SPI and x8/x16 parallel options, depending on the device. Toggle products operate from a 3.3V supply. On applicable Toggle parts, Everspin specifies 20 years of data retention and unlimited read/write endurance. Once a write is complete, the data is already non-volatile; the device can write new data to the same location without first erasing a sector or block. For systems that regularly update configuration settings, counters, logs or operating state, that changes how power loss has to be handled. The data remains in memory when power is removed without requiring a battery, capacitor or separate STORE operation. There is no need to detect a power failure and move the latest information from SRAM into non-volatile memory before the available energy runs out. Those characteristics are one reason Toggle MRAM continues to be used in mission-critical applications across industrial controls, factory automation, metering, transportation, medical equipment and aerospace and defense systems. It fits especially well when the memory footprint is modest, writes happen frequently and the design needs an established interface over a long product life. Its non-volatility also helps preserve critical data through unexpected power loss. Where STT-MRAM changes the equation STT-MRAM moves into a different density, voltage and interface range. Everspin's PERSYST EMxxLX family operates at 1.8V and supports Single, Dual, Quad and Octal SPI modes, depending on the device. The portfolio extends through 256Mb, and applicable Octal devices support operation up to 200 MHz with throughput up to 400 MB/s. The devices support byte-level writes and can rewrite a location without an erase operation. That matters in applications where code, configuration or other persistent data may need to be updated frequently. Endurance and retention vary by device. For example, the 128Mb EM128LX specifies 10^14 writes per 32-byte memory location and a minimum 10-year data retention period across temperature. The higher densities and faster serial interfaces suit applications with larger code or data footprints than the current Toggle portfolio can address. STT-MRAM can support larger boot-code and data footprints, FPGA configuration, industrial computing and embedded systems that need higher serial bandwidth. A recent design win shows how that can work in a real system. Astro Digital selected Everspin's 64Mb PERSYST STT-MRAM as the primary fail-safe memory for the boot process on an upcoming Raven bus geosynchronous Earth orbit satellite mission. The memory retains essential boot information without power and provides fast access during startup or recovery. Everspin also offers a 1Gb ST-DDR4 STT-MRAM product for high-bandwidth persistent-memory applications. That device belongs to the same underlying STT-MRAM technology family, but it addresses a different architectural problem than and should be evaluated separately. A practical comparison Where the decision usually gets made Interface and voltage can narrow the field quickly A system built around a 3.3V asynchronous parallel bus starts from a very different point than one designed around a 1.8V Octal SPI interface. That matters in a new design, but it can matter even more during a migration. A 3.3V host may need level translation to work with a 1.8V STT-MRAM device. Toggle and STT-MRAM should not be treated as board-level drop-in alternatives simply because both are non-volatile MRAM. Density is only part of the workload A few kilobits of calibration data and 128Mb of boot code clearly point to different devices. Write activity can be just as important in the applications that fall between those extremes. A system that updates counters, event records or state information continuously puts different demands on memory than one that writes configuration data only occasionally. Toggle MRAM's unlimited endurance is particularly useful in high-cycle applications. STT-MRAM brings larger densities and higher serial bandwidth while still supporting frequent persistent writes. Retention, temperature and qualification vary by part number It is tempting to describe Toggle or STT-MRAM as if every device in each family carries the same environmental specifications. They do not. Temperature range, data retention and qualification status vary by product. Match those requirements to the specific part under consideration, especially in automotive, aerospace, defense and other high-reliability systems. The memory being replaced changes the conversation NOR flash migrations often start with erase behavior, write performance, endurance and the amount of firmware work required to change the memory architecture. Battery-backed SRAM presents another problem. The goal may be to keep data persistent through power loss without depending on a battery and its maintenance, size and end-of-life considerations. nvSRAM is different again. Persistence is already part of the architecture, so migration can affect interface timing, STORE/RECALL behavior used to move data between volatile and non-volatile storage and how much existing hardware or firmware needs to change. Those are different starting points and MRAM can address each of them. Both Toggle and STT-MRAM can serve as drop-in replacements, often requiring little or no hardware redesign. MRAM combines non-volatility with fast write performance and high endurance, making it well suited for applications with frequent updates, high system availability and long-term data retention. It can also provide designers with an additional qualified memory option to help reduce supply chain risk. For more information, read this application note . Why both remain in the portfolio Everspin continues to develop and sell both Toggle and STT-MRAM because customers are solving different memory problems. A 3.3V embedded system that needs a few megabits of persistent memory and expects very high write activity may point naturally toward Toggle MRAM. A 1.8V design that needs a larger memory footprint, xSPI connectivity and more serial bandwidth may point toward STT-MRAM. Plenty of applications fall somewhere between those examples. The useful comparison starts with the actual system: how much memory it needs, how the host connects to it, how often the data changes, how long it must be retained and where the product has to operate. If a design falls in the overlap between the two families, Everspin's application team can help compare the specific parts and requirements, rather than assuming one MRAM technology is the answer for every system.

articles.summary: AIM Fellows Complete Summer Experience mboyle Thu, 09/24/2026 - 12:09 Post Image September 24, 2026 - A dozen college educators representing schools across the country are back on campus and better positioned to discuss the intricacies of mining with their students. A group of 12 higher education faculty members recently completed Freeport’s Academic-Industry Mining (AIM) Fellowship, an experiential learning opportunity intended to provide participants firsthand insight into modern mining practices they can bring back into the classroom. Through the program, educators spent at least six weeks working alongside Freeport employees, contributing to projects aligned with their academic interests. The fellowship is designed not only to provide practical industry experience but also to help those educators better prepare the next generation of mining professionals. The goal of this program is to help create “a pipeline to our future workforce,” said Angie Harmon, Regional Manager of Social Performance-North America. This year, the groundwork for that pipeline was laid with the help of 12 educators from universities across the U.S., including Kate Brown Requist, an assistant professor of mining engineering at Tennessee State University, and Azeem Raza, an assistant research professor at Missouri University of Science and Technology. Other participating universities included Arizona State University, Colorado School of Mines, Michigan Technological University, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, University of Arizona and West Virginia University. In addition to working on projects related to their own areas of expertise, the fellows also had the opportunity to visit Freeport operations and meet with employees across the business. Those experiences included attending a Reinvent Mining meeting in Phoenix and a visit to Tucson, where they toured the Technology Center and Sierrita mine, getting a closer look at the processes and technology behind the mining industry today. Brown Requist said the opportunity offered a valuable look at just how much Freeport is helping shape the future of the mining industry. “It was very eye-opening,” Brown Requist said. “There’s a lot going on at Freeport, and this was an opportunity to see what that leading edge of innovation looks like and how the company is leveraging analytics. It’s a great example to show my students what modernizing and digitizing the mining industry really looks like.” Raza’s opportunities were more connected to the company’s innovation deployment. With an interest in how mine design will evolve and adopt technologies like artificial intelligence, automation and robotics as they become more specialized and commonplace in mining, Raza was given the opportunity to visit the company’s Bagdad mine, where he saw firsthand how Freeport is leading the industry’s adoption of autonomous haulage in the U.S. “Bagdad is a very exciting location,” Raza said. “It is clear Freeport is looking to the future and is optimizing its operations for that. Autonomous haulage, robotics, artificial intelligence – these are the topics that should attract the next generation, and now I can help prepare them to contribute more significantly.” Photos (top and bottom): Kate Brown Requist got a closer look at Arizona’s geology during a visit to the company’s Sierrita mine; During their time with Freeport, Azeem Raza and the other fellows toured the labs at Technology Center Tucson.
articles.title: AIM Fellows Complete Summer Experience
